Lett played [[college football]] for the [[Emporia State Hornets football|Emporia State Hornets]] and was selected in the seventh round of the [[1991 NFL draft]] by the Cowboys, where he spent 10 seasons. During his final season in 2001, he played for the [[Denver Broncos]]. With the Cowboys, Lett received two [[Pro Bowl]] selections and won three [[Super Bowl]] titles. He is also remembered for two botched plays—a fumble before scoring a touchdown in [[Super Bowl XXVII]] and a failed recovery after a blocked field goal in a [[NFL on Thanksgiving Day|Thanksgiving game]]—although he would help his team win the Super Bowl in both seasons. After retiring, Lett served as the assistant defensive line coach for the Cowboys from 2011 to 2022.

'''Leonard Barnett Davis''' (born September 5, 1978) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[Guard (American football)|guard]] for 12 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL).  He was a consensus [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] playing [[college football]] for the [[Texas Longhorns football|Texas Longhorns]], where he was also a two-time [[Outland Trophy]] finalist and a [[Lombardi Award]] semifinalist. Davis was selected by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] with the second overall pick in the [[2001 NFL draft]]. He played for the Cardinals, the [[Dallas Cowboys]] - where he was a three-time Pro-Bowler and a second team All-Pro - and the [[San Francisco 49ers]], with whom he went to [[Super Bowl XLVII]]. He also spent part of a season with the [[Detroit Lions]], but never took the field for them.

He currently works as a radio personality in Jacksonville, Florida. {{NFL predraft | height ft = 6 | height in = 3 1/4 | weight = 296 | dash = 5.19 | ten split = 1.91 | twenty split = 3.08 | shuttle = 4.50 | vertical = 25.0 | arm span = 34 1/2 | hand span = 9 1/2 }} Searcy is a former [[National Football League|NFL]] [[offensive lineman]] who played primarily for the [[Pittsburgh Steelers]] and [[Jacksonville Jaguars]] in an 11-year career spanning from 1992 to 2002. He was drafted in the first-round and 11th overall by the Pittsburgh Steelers following his graduation from the [[University of Miami]] in the [[1992 NFL draft]].{{Cite web |title=1992 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1992/draft.htm |access-date=2023-05-07 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}} This was the first draft pick in the post-Chuck Noll era. Beginning in 1993 (his second year), Searcy was installed at the right tackle position.{{cite news|last=Bouchette|first=Ed|title=BGI Fan Q&A with Ed Bouchette|url=http://www.post-gazette.com/stories/sports/steelers/bgi-fan-qa-with-ed-bouchette-559489/|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=March 19, 2012}} He stayed in this position until he left the team for the Jacksonville Jaguars as a free agent in 1996.{{cite news|last=Huffman|first=Dane|title=Panthers Make Use of Mistfits|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1129&dat=19970109&id=X9BRAAAAIBAJ&sjid=KW8DAAAAIBAJ&pg=3978,4805912|newspaper=Pittsburgh Post-Gazette|date=January 9, 1997}} In the 2000 offseason, Searcy tore his right quadriceps muscle and spent the entire 2000 season on injured reserve. In 2001 Searcy signed a six year, $31.5 million contract with the [[Baltimore Ravens]] in 2001 where he would tear his left triceps tendon in preseason and miss his second straight full season due to injury.{{cite news|title=Searcy suffers serious triceps injury|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/2001/08/05/Searcy-suffers-serious-triceps-injury/3002996984000/|newspaper=UPI|date=August 5, 2001}} The Ravens would waive Searcy following the 2001 season and he'd be signed by [[Miami Dolphins]] during the 2002 offseason. Searcy once again dealt with injury concerns as he'd tear his right triceps while warming up for a preseason game against the [[Chicago Bears]] and was cut by the Dolphins prior to the regular season rather than being sent to the injured reserve for the third straight year in a row.{{cite news|title=Dolphins release injured Searcy|url=https://www.sun-sentinel.com/2002/09/02/dolphins-release-injured-searcy/|newspaper=UPI|date=September 2, 2002}} He would never be signed to an NFL roster again after missing three straight seasons due to injuries following his lone All-Pro season in 1999. From 2004 to 2006, Searcy was the offensive line coach at [[Florida International University]] in [[Miami, Florida]]. Searcy was interviewed about his time at the University of Miami for the documentary ''[[The U (film)|The U]]'', which premiered December 12, 2009 on [[ESPN]]. Searcy also appeared in the episode "Broke," part of [[ESPN]]'s ''[[30 for 30]]'' series of sports documentaries discussing the high percentage of professional athletes who suffer financial problems. He gave details on an incident in which a girlfriend stole $600,000 from him.

He started at defensive end in [[Super Bowl XXV]] and [[Super Bowl XXVI|XXVI]].{{citation needed|date=March 2010}} He retired after the 1992 season with the [[Philadelphia Eagles]].<ref name="pfr"/>

Seals currently lives in [[Clinton, Mississippi]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Prep notebook: Former NFL player Leon Seals to return to Scotlandville in NFL initiative |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/new_orleans/sports/high_schools/article_6dca81ee-91c3-597d-bdee-6f7787223918.html |website=The New Orleans Advocate |date=October 16, 2015 |accessdate=August 21, 2018}}</ref> He has served as a member of the Hinds County Sheriff's Department.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Posey |first1=Shanderia K. |title=Sworn in to serve |url=http://themississippilink.com/2016/01/07/sworn-in-to-serve/ |website=The Mississippi Link |accessdate=August 21, 2018 |date=January 7, 2016}}</ref>

'''Leon "Pop" Bright, Jr.''' (born May 19, 1955 in [[Starke, Florida]]) is a former [[Gridiron football]] player in the [[Canadian Football League]] for four years and in the [[National Football League]] for five years.

He played Jr high school ball at Thomas Jefferson Jr High,  [[high school football]] at [[Merritt Island High School]] in [[Merritt Island, Florida]] and was on the 1972 Merritt Island High, Florida Class AAAA state championship team.  Bright was named to the [[FHSAA's All-Century Team]] which selected the Top 33 players in the 100-year history of high school football in the state of Florida's history.<ref>{{cite web |date=December 12, 2007 |title=FHSAA announces 33-member All-Century football team |url=http://www.fhsaa.org/news/2007/1212.htm |url-status=dead |archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20091227201709/http://www.fhsaa.org/news/2007/1212.htm |archivedate=2009-12-27 |accessdate=2010-01-26 |website=FHSAA}}</ref>

He played [[college football]] at [[Florida State University]] where he still holds the record for most yards on a kickoff return, which resulted in a touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://seminoles.cstv.com/auto_pdf/p_hotos/s_chools/fsu/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/02offenserecords |title=Florida State University Official Athletic Site |access-date=2008-10-23 |archive-date=2009-01-01 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090101111631/http://seminoles.cstv.com/auto_pdf/p_hotos/s_chools/fsu/sports/m-footbl/auto_pdf/02offenserecords |url-status=dead }}</ref>

From 1977-1980, Bright played [[running back]], [[wide receiver]], [[defensive back]], and [[kickoff returner]] for the [[BC Lions]].<ref>"B.C. Can’t Find Bright", ''[[Leader-Post]]'' (March 18, 1981).</ref><ref>"Move to Big Apple Pays off For Bright", ''[[Star-Phoenix]]'' (December 19, 1981).</ref>

He also played for the [[New York Giants]] from 1981–1983, serving as the team's primary punt returner. He was with the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] from 1984-1985.

Bright was selected to the Lions' 2004 50th Anniversary Dream Team.  In 2006, he was the head coach for the [[Daytona Beach Thunder]] arena football team.

Leon also runs the Leon Bright Charitable Foundation. His foundation works with underprivileged kids and families.

He is the eldest of 10 children and also the eldest of 23 paternal grandchildren.  Bright and wife, Tammy, currently reside in [[Volusia County]], Florida.  He has four children and four grandchildren.{{Citation needed|date=May 2009}}
